changes.title: feat(llm): carry the four format rules the customer prompt left out
changes.description:
## What does this PR do?

Four rules of the customer output format now reach the model. They were written
down, they are judged, and the prompt did not carry them.

```
+ Every entry that asks something of the reader stands above every entry that
+ does not, whichever group each of them sits in. One such entry below one that
+ asks nothing is wrong even when the groups themselves are in order. A breaking
+ change comes first of all.
+ Nothing follows the last group. A migration link belongs in its entry, not in
+ a closing line.

+ Changes the reader would not act on are gathered into one closing bullet of
+ their group, opening with "Also:", rather than each taking a bullet of its
+ own. That bullet is one entry and carries the observation alone: the three
+ parts below do not apply to it.

+ A claim of degree - faster, smaller, higher, more reliable - needs something
+ in the entry the reader can check it against. Without a number or a basis,
+ leave the claim out rather than soften it.
```

Each is pinned by a test, as the rules around them are.

## Why?

Measured on the rendering of 2026-09-04, judged against the frozen customer
criterion in goldbarth/chartula-evals. Two of the four failed that document:

- An entry saying separate marketing files are no longer written, which costs a
  reader who relies on them, sat below entries that ask nothing.
- "defaults to a much higher value" is a claim of degree with nothing to check
  it against. The rule next to it forbids superlatives and marketing language,
  and that phrase is neither, so it passed.

A document axis failing makes the whole rendering unshippable however good the
entries are. The rendering shipped 8 of 19 entries and does not ship as a whole,
and these two are the cheapest part of that to close: the rules exist and are
already agreed, they only had to arrive.

Closes #111

## Notes for review

- **The `Also:` line carries its own exemption.** #106 made the outcome slot
  compulsory; `output-format.md` rule 11 says the collapsed line usually has no
  outcome at all. The sentence "carries the observation alone: the three parts
  below do not apply to it" is what keeps the prompt from holding two rules that
  contradict each other.
- **Ordering is stated across the document, not within a group.** That is what
  the axis judges: a group named "What needs action" can stand at the top while
  an entry that asks something sits three groups below it.
- **Not in scope:** the outcome wording, which fails 10 of 19 entries and needs a
  different formulation rather than a rule that is missing, and the coverage rule
  behind the A1 failure, which is already in the prompt in full. Both are their
  own turn, so their effect can be read on their own axis.

changes.title: feat(cli): warn at startup when a run has no GitHub token
changes.description:
## What does this PR do?

A run that starts without a GitHub token now says so before it does any work, on stderr:

```
Warning: no GitHub token found in GITHUB_TOKEN - the run continues unauthenticated.
  GitHub allows 60 requests an hour per IP address without one, and a run
  spends roughly one per pull request, so a release can exhaust the budget
  partway through. A token raises the limit to 5000.
  Set one with: export GITHUB_TOKEN=$(gh auth token)
```

The run is not refused - a token is optional and a small release fits the anonymous budget. The message names whichever variable the run actually reads, so it stays true when `github.tokenEnvironmentVariable` was renamed, and it goes to stderr so redirecting the changelog to a file keeps it out.

`README.md` and `docs/configuration.md` now state the practical limit instead of only listing the variable.

## Why?

Closes #89.

Without a token GitHub allows 60 requests an hour per IP address, and Chartula spends roughly one per pull request. Nothing said so. The run started silently, and when the budget ran out it failed partway through with a 403 that names a commit:

```
Error: GitHub API returned 403 rate limit exceeded for commit 8061f468...
API rate limit exceeded for <ip>. (But here's the good news: Authenticated requests get a higher rate limit.)
```

The cause is one environment variable, but nothing on that path points at it - and the budget is shared with everything else reaching GitHub from that address, so the failure can arrive on a first run.

Verified against this repository: without a token the warning is printed and the run then hits the same 403 as before; with a token set, nothing is printed.

changes.title: fix(output): keep the rendering when the description is all the model wrote
changes.description:
## What does this PR do?

`ReleaseDescription.SplitOff` no longer lifts a description out when there is
nothing under it. If striking the labelled first line would leave an empty body,
the line was not a description: the text stays the body and the description is
`null`.

```csharp
// before: "Description: All there is."  ->  ("All there is.", "")
// after:  "Description: All there is."  ->  (null, "Description: All there is.")
```

Everything else about the split is unchanged. A labelled line with one entry
under it still splits, a bolded label still counts, and text without the label is
still all body.

## Why?

The first run made after #104 produced a customer rendering of zero characters
and no `release-<tag>.md`, and reported no error:

```
technical  26320 characters
customer       0 characters
product     4327 characters
```

The run before it, on the same release and the same fact base, produced 25,457
characters of customer text.

The model was called - the run metrics report three rephrasing calls - and the
answer was then lifted out whole as the description, leaving an empty body.
From there every step behaved as designed: an empty customer body means a
release with nothing to say to that audience, so no page is written and nothing
is flagged. The rendering was gone and the run looked clean.

Ruled out on the way: the no-statements path in `ReleaseChangelogGenerator`
makes no call at all, `ChangelogFormatter` only normalises line endings and
bullet markers, `ReviewCoordinator` passes the text through while review is off,
and the customer prompt is intact. `SplitOff` is the only consumer of the
customer text that #104 added.

This does not decide why the model answered the way it did. It decides that the
answer survives either way, so the next run can be read rather than guessed at.

Closes #108

## Notes for review

- **The guard turns on the body, not on the description.** A label line with an
  empty description and entries under it keeps its existing behaviour: the line
  is consumed, the field is omitted. That case is a model leaving the line out as
  asked, which is not this one.
- **The pinning test was inverted, not deleted.**
  `A_description_on_its_own_leaves_an_empty_body` asserted the behaviour this
  fixes. It is now
  `A_line_with_nothing_under_it_is_the_body_and_not_a_description`, carrying the
  run that produced it in a comment.
- **Not in scope:** that an empty customer rendering passes through the pipeline
  without a word. It is correct for a release that genuinely has nothing for that
  audience, and telling the two apart is a separate change.

changes.title: fix(llm): require the outcome slot instead of allowing it to be dropped
changes.description:
## What does this PR do?

The customer prompt now requires the outcome of an entry — what the reader can
now rely on — instead of listing it among the parts that may be dropped. Two
rules change in `ChangelogPromptBuilder.Prompts.cs`:

- The four-part rule allowed *any of the last three* parts to be left out, the
  outcome among them. Only the second (who or what it applies to) and the fourth
  (what the reader has to do) may be absent now.
- The outcome test ended in "Say what the reader can now rely on instead, or
  leave it out", which offered a way past the test it had just set. It now reads
  "Striking the clause is not the way out."

## Why?

Measured on the rendering of 2026-09-03: seven of twenty entries fail C3, one of
them with no outcome sentence at all. The format described an entry as four
parts and then permitted three of them to be dropped, so an entry without an
outcome was following the prompt rather than breaking it — and the escape hatch
in the outcome test made striking the clause the cheapest repair.

Figures and the full reading live in `goldbarth/chartula-evals`,
`docs/measurements.md`. No related issue.

changes.title: feat(output): write the customer rendering as a page of its own
changes.description:
## What does this PR do?

A run now writes `release-<tag>.md`: the customer rendering as a page you can publish, in the published serialisation from [`docs/output-format.md`](https://github.com/goldbarth/chartula-evals/blob/main/docs/output-format.md) - YAML front matter, then the entries.

```markdown
---
title: Release 0.1.0
description: Chartula runs end to end on a repository, from pull requests to notes for three audiences.
publishedAt: 2026-09-03
---

### What's New
...
```

Every field has a source, and a field whose source has nothing to give is left out rather than filled in:

| Field | Source | Absent when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `title` | the tag | never - a page without a tag is not composed |
| `description` | the model, from the release's facts | the facts do not support a sentence |
| `publishedAt` | the date the tag was made | git gives nothing readable |
| `tags` | labels on the pull requests | always, for now - see #98 |

Also in this change:

- **The tag date reaches the pipeline.** `GitCliCommitReader` reads `creatordate` - the tagger date for an annotated tag, the commit date for a lightweight one - and `CommitRange` carries it. It is nullable rather than defaulted to today, because an invented date is worse than an absent field.
- **The description is written in the same call as the entries.** It is a rephrasing of facts already in front of the model, so a second call would buy nothing, and the faithfulness check covers it on the same footing as the text: the pipeline checks the description together with the body rather than beside it. The prompt asks for the line under `ReleaseDescription.Label` and the parser reads the same constant back, so a reworded prompt cannot silently lose the field.
- **A preview shows the description it would publish**, so the one field a preview could not vouch for is no longer the one that opens the page.
- **A release with no customer entries produces no page**, rather than a page with an empty body.
- **The page is written under `--no-publish`** like the other local outputs. Writing a file a person could publish is not publishing it, so there is nothing for that flag to hold back.

## Why?

The customer rendering was generated, checked for faithfulness, reviewed - and then written nowhere. It existed only as a field inside `changelog.json`, so the audience the tool exists for had no output a person could publish, and a consumer had to read the JSON and build the page themselves, which is the work the tool is supposed to have done.

Measured, not assumed: on the rendering of 2026-09-03 the evaluation harness fails the grouping axis on the missing opening, and the same document with front matter prepended by hand passes it with nothing else changed.

Closes #103

## Notes for review

- **`changelog.json` is unchanged.** The description lives on the page and not in the record, so a fixture replayed from `changelog.json` cannot reconstruct the page's opening. Carrying per-audience metadata in the JSON is a shape decision of its own and would touch the documented format; it is not needed for a publishable file and is left out here deliberately rather than overlooked.
- **The description is not presented for review.** Review returns one string, so the body is what a reviewer edits. The description still goes through the faithfulness check and is printed in the run's output.
- **Out of scope, as the issue says:** the product audience (no written template), the file serialisation of the customer rendering (many releases in one document), where the file is written to beyond the working directory, and #98.

changes.title: feat(output): write a run's artefacts without publishing a release
changes.description:
## What does this PR do?

Adds `chartula generate --no-publish`. It writes `changelog.json` and `CHANGELOG.md` and leaves the release notes untouched, and the run names what it skipped next to what it wrote:

```
Wrote:
  - changelog.json
  - CHANGELOG.md
Skipped (--no-publish):
  - Release notes for v1.0.0 in octo/repo
```

Without the flag nothing changes: `generate` writes and publishes, `preview` writes nothing.

## Why?

A run either wrote nothing or wrote everything and published. `changelog.json` is not a by-product - it is the only machine-readable record of what a run was given and what it produced - and getting it should not require announcing a release for the tag. Where no release exists yet, `GitHubReleaseNotesWriter` creates one, so today a `generate` against this repository would publish its first release as a side effect of producing a record.

That blocks two things: measuring a prompt change means rendering the same release repeatedly, and every one of those runs would rewrite the public release notes of a tag that is not being re-released; and #95 asks for a `CHANGELOG.md` explicitly without a GitHub release.

Closes #100

## How it works

- `PipelineMode` gains a third value, `GenerateWithoutPublishing`. The mode already documents itself as "how a pipeline run treats its outputs", which is exactly what differs here - so no third verb, and nothing new on `ReleaseRequest`.
- `ReleasePipeline.WriteOutputsAsync` writes the two files in both generate modes and calls `IReleaseNotesWriter` only for `Generate`. What it left out goes into the new `ReleaseOutcome.SkippedOutputs` (an `init` property defaulting to `[]`, so existing construction is unchanged).
- CLI: `CommandLineArguments.HasFlag`, plus `Program.ParseMode(command, args)` so the flag-to-mode mapping is testable, and the help text is now a `Program.Usage` string a test can hold to what the CLI accepts.

One judgement call the issue left open: `preview --no-publish` stays an ordinary preview rather than an error. Preview publishes nothing anyway, so the flag's promise holds, and the tool does not validate unknown flags elsewhere.

## Type of change

- [x] New feature
- [ ] Documentation
- [ ] Refactor / internal
- [ ] Breaking change

- [x] Code follows the formatting in `.editorconfig`
- [x] I've added or updated tests where it makes sense
- [x] I've updated documentation where relevant
- [x] No secrets or API keys are included in this change

`dotnet build -c Release` is warning-free; `dotnet test -c Release` is green at 326 tests, 7 of them new. The new tests assert that the release notes writer is not called with the flag and is called exactly once without it, that the skipped publication is named in the outcome and printed, that the flag maps to the right mode, and that `--help` names it.

changes.title: fix(llm): state the shape of a customer entry instead of leaving it to the model
changes.description:
Part of #96. Customer audience only - see *What this does not do* below, and please do not let it auto-close the issue.

## What

The customer audience carried one sentence about tone and nothing about shape:

```csharp
private const string AudienceCustomer =
    "Audience: Customer. Focus on what changed for the user in plain language.";
```

It now carries the shape as well: the groups and their order, that every fact arriving has to be carried, the entry built from four parts, the openings that are not allowed, whose knowledge the reader may be assumed to have, and where a setting has to be named.

## Why these rules and not others

Each one answers a failure that was counted, not one that seemed likely. The evaluation harness scored 53 entries across three renderings by hand and then with a judge; the figures are in [`docs/targets.md`](https://github.com/goldbarth/chartula-evals/blob/main/docs/targets.md) and the rules themselves in [`docs/output-format.md`](https://github.com/goldbarth/chartula-evals/blob/main/docs/output-format.md).

| Failure | Count | Rule added |
|---|---|---|
| The closing clause restates the opening instead of stating an outcome | 19 of 53 | the strike test |
| An expression only a contributor would know | 15 of 53 | how the reader would have met it |
| The entry opens on the work that was done | 8 of 53 | the forbidden openings, named |
| An option announced with nowhere to act on it | 8 of 53 | the place, or leave the option out |
| A change carried by no entry at all | every rendering | carry every fact that arrives |
| An entry that asks something, below entries that do not | 2 of 3 | route it into the first group |
| Entries running on past their outcome | every rendering | two sentences, and stop at the outcome |

Not one of the three renderings ships whole, and four models do not differ in kind - which is the point. This was never a model choosing badly.

## Two decisions worth reviewing

**Two clauses are tests, not lists.** What counts as an outcome, and what counts as an expression the reader has already met. A list of forbidden cases is never finished, and the first case outside it gets the wrong verdict - naming the outcome slot alone had already produced *"so text completes properly"*, which is the opening negated.

**No category is named.** `categories.names` lets a user rename any category and `GroundedFactsFactory` prefixes each fact with the configured display name, so a rule saying *"a fix goes to Bug Fixes"* would break for whoever renamed `Fix`. The groups are defined by what a change is instead. For the same reason the prompt does not restate which changes appear at all: the user-visible filter in `GroundedFactsFactory` already decides that, and putting it in prose too would be the same rule in two places.

## Tests

Fourteen new tests, asserting shape rather than content - the acceptance criterion the old ones could not meet, since they would not have caught any of the three variants in the issue.

Eleven fail if the format block is removed. The other three are guards: Technical and Product stay untouched, the content rules still apply to every audience, and no category is named. Whitespace is collapsed before asserting, so a rule can be re-wrapped without breaking a test.

```
dotnet build -c Release    0 warnings, 0 errors
dotnet test  -c Release    330 passed
```

## What this does not do

- **Technical and Product are untouched.** They state tone alone, because they have no written specification. Inventing a shape for an audience nobody has specified would be the same defect as leaving it to the model, only harder to notice. Two of the issue's acceptance criteria stay open for them, including the Keep a Changelog question.
- **It does not yet prove reproducibility across runs and models.** That is the second acceptance criterion and it is a measurement, not a claim. The next step is to re-render v0.1.0 with this prompt and count against the seven figures above; `judge/count.py` in the harness does that without anyone labelling by hand.

- [x] Builds without warnings
- [x] All tests pass
- [x] One concern
- [x] No debug or commented-out code left behind
- [x] Describes what changed and why, and links the issue

Adds a section to the README pointing at [chartula-evals](https://github.com/goldbarth/chartula-evals), the repository that holds the evaluation side: cases, run costs across models, and the criterion the generated text is judged by.

changes.title: feat(llm): add an OpenAI-compatible provider with a configurable base URL
changes.description:
Closes #78.

`llm.provider` accepted one value, so the key documented a choice the user did not have. It now accepts `openai-compatible`, which reaches any endpoint speaking the OpenAI chat-completions dialect - hosted ones that are cheaper, and a server on the user's own machine, where release data never leaves it.

## What

- `LlmProvider` + `LlmProviderParser`, in the shape `ThinkingMode` already uses. An unknown name throws rather than falling back, because silently reaching a different provider would send release data somewhere the user did not choose.
- `LlmProviderDefaults` takes the defaults out of the property initializers. A default that is right for one provider is wrong for the other.
- `llm.baseUrl`, applying to **both** providers - `AnthropicClient.BaseUrl` exists, and a proxy in front of the Anthropic API is the same need.
- `OpenAiCompatibleChatClient` is the only place the OpenAI package is named, which is what keeps it out of the domain.

## Decisions worth disagreeing with

**Neither `model` nor `baseUrl` has a default for `openai-compatible`.** The models an endpoint serves are its own. The endpoint is the more deliberate omission: a default would have to be a hosted one, and this provider exists so release data can stay on the user's machine - anyone configuring only the model would then send it off the machine without being asked. Both errors name the missing key and give an example.

**A missing API key builds a client anyway.** Ollama, LM Studio, llama.cpp and vLLM do not read the Authorization header. `ApiKeyCredential` rejects an empty string in its constructor, so a placeholder stands in - otherwise "no key needed" becomes a crash before any request goes out. A hosted endpoint sees the placeholder and answers 401, which is the point: the refusal comes from the endpoint, as it already did for Anthropic.

**`thinking` is refused rather than dropped.** It travels in an Anthropic request type. Handing that to another client fails on the first call; refusing at startup fails where the setting was made.

## Native AOT

Trimmer publish, `linux-x64`, self-contained, on 2026-08-03:

| | baseline | with this change | delta |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| trim warnings | 1230 | 1230 | **0** |
| publish size | 29.70 MB | 31.40 MB | +1.63 MiB (+5.7%) |

This inverts the expectation in the issue. Of the 1230 warnings, **1204 come from `Anthropic.*`** and 24 from YamlDotNet; this package adds none, because the OpenAI SDK serializes through `System.ClientModel` with hand-written readers rather than reflection. The only new transitive dependency on net10.0 is `System.ClientModel` - not Azure.Core. The already-shipped provider SDK is the AOT blocker, not this one.

Caveat: a trimmer run is not a native AOT run. `clang` is absent on the machine, so there is no native binary size and `IL3050` from package assemblies is unmeasured.

## Two things found by running it

**`NetworkTimeout` raised to 10 minutes.** The SDK default is 100 seconds - fine for a hosted API, wrong for the case this provider exists for. Against a local 14B model it killed two of three audience texts, each after four retries.

**The base URL scheme is checked, not just the parse.** `localhost:11434` parses as an absolute URI whose scheme is `localhost` and whose path is `11434`. A forgotten `http://` would have surfaced far from the setting that caused it.

## Smoke runs

Three runs against Ollama 0.21.0 on 2026-08-03, `v0.1.0` of this repository:

| Model | Context | Thorough claims | Rule-based claims | Tokens |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `qwen2.5-coder:7b` | 4096 (default) | 3 | 2 | 26,232 |
| `qwen2.5:14b` | 4096 (default) | 0 | 8 | 26,303 |
| `qwen2.5:14b` | 24576 | 1 | 34 | 78,448 |

The first two measured a broken configuration rather than the models. Ollama truncated every prompt from ~12,400 tokens to 4,096, and since the instruction sits at the front while truncation keeps the end, the model received the text under review with neither the facts nor the task. Raising the context produced a usable changelog from the same model.

Two findings were filed rather than fixed here: #85 (a truncated prompt must fail the run) and #86 (a thorough check that never saw the facts must not report as clean).

**AC 6 is only half met.** The hosted smoke run is outstanding - it needs a key, and it is the one that exercises the real key path, HTTPS, and an endpoint that does *not* enforce the schema by constrained decoding. Recorded as an open item on #78 rather than quietly dropped.

## On #79

Its trigger did not fire: Ollama held the JSON schema on every call. Precisely, though - it *enforces* the schema by constrained decoding rather than the model following it; a request for a poem, sent with the verdict schema, came back as a valid verdict. The poor text quality is **not** a #79 trigger, since a native adapter would not have changed it. That was the context window. One runner, two models: LM Studio, llama.cpp and vLLM stay unverified.

## Tests

12 new, 315 green. No test covers `NetworkTimeout` - it is an SDK-internal option observable only through a genuinely slow response, and a test reproducing that would tie the suite's runtime to a timeout.

changes.title: feat: make thinking a decision instead of a default
changes.description:
## What does this PR do?

Adds `llm.thinking`, with the same three states the provider has: `provider-default` (the default), `disabled`, `adaptive`.

Chartula sent no `thinking` field at all, and the models disagree about what that silence means. Measured on the same release, same command, 2026-07-31 ([full evidence](https://github.com/goldbarth/chartula/issues/77#issuecomment-5143594770)):

| Model | Thinks by default | Total tokens | Cost | Thorough-check output | Claims found |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `claude-haiku-4-5` | no | 92,148 | $0.12 | 238 | 7 |
| `claude-sonnet-5` | **yes** | 156,706 | $0.55 | 6,982 | 0 |
| `claude-opus-4-8` | no | 132,983 | $0.89 | 69 | 0 |
| `claude-opus-5` | **yes** | 156,221 | $1.34 | 4,967 | 0 |

The thorough check is the clean signal: its payload is a near-empty JSON verdict, so 69 output tokens on Opus 4.8 against 4,967 on Opus 5 for the identical answer of zero claims is reasoning being billed, not output. Opus 5 and Opus 4.8 cost the same per token, and the run still costs 50% more.

Closes #82

## Why?

Not because thinking is wrong — because it was never a decision. The cost of a run depended on a default that varies by model, in a project where prompt iteration is the priority and every iteration is paid for.

The default deliberately keeps today's behavior. There is no evidence for moving it yet: zero claims found with thinking, zero without, across one clean release. The switch is what makes the next measurement possible — a single Opus 5 run with `thinking: disabled` against the Opus 5 run already recorded, for about $1.

### How it travels without dragging the provider into the domain

Thinking has no provider-agnostic field in `Microsoft.Extensions.AI`, so it rides `ChatOptions.RawRepresentationFactory`, which the Anthropic adapter reads.

That would normally mean naming the Anthropic request type where the request is built — inside `Chartula.Core`, which deliberately does not reference a provider package (`docs/architecture.md:58`). So `ChatModelOptions` carries a `Func<IChatClient, object?>` and nothing more; `AnthropicThinking` in the composition root is the only place that knows what that object is. The domain still cannot see a provider type.

`MessageCreateParams` has required members the adapter fills in itself, so the fragment carries placeholders for model, messages and the ceiling. Their only job is to satisfy the compiler.

A run with `thinking: disabled` and a deliberately invalid model answered `model: placeholder` on all three audiences - the placeholder *was* the request. changes.title: fix: tell an unreadable thorough check from a clean one
changes.description:
## What does this PR do?

Makes a thorough check that could not be read say so, instead of looking exactly like a check that found nothing.

Reproduced first, with the real pipeline, the real `ChatModel` and the real `ThoroughFaithfulnessChecker`; only the `IChatClient` was a stand-in answering `"Sorry, I cannot produce JSON here."`:

```text
Technical: success=True, flags=0
Customer: success=True, flags=0
Product: success=True, flags=0
Run metrics
  Rule-based check: 3 runs, 0 with findings, 0 claims, no tokens
  Thorough check:   3 runs, 0 with findings, 0 claims, 0 in / 0 out
    caught 0 claims the rule-based check missed, for 0 tokens in 3 calls
```

Three checks ran, three parses failed, and the summary reports that the thorough check found nothing - when it read nothing. The run is clean and the tokens are spent.

After:

```text
  Thorough check:   3 runs, 0 with findings, 0 claims, 6,230 in / 130 out
    3 of 3 runs came back unreadable and verified nothing
```

plus a flag on each affected audience text, so review mode shows it too.

## Why?

`IsFaithful` was the intended signal for exactly this and **nothing read it** - `grep` found only the places that constructed it. `ReleasePipeline.CollectFlagsAsync` consumes the claim list alone, so three different states arrived as the same empty list: checked and clean, checked with nothing found, and never checked at all.

Same shape as the truncation bug in #70: a failure that reports success. It is present with Anthropic today, and it is a precondition for the fail-loud provider contract decided in #75, since a weaker model is the likeliest source of an unusable answer.

Closes #76

### What changed, and why that shape

- **`FaithfulnessReport` carries a `Status`** - `Checked`, `NotEvaluated`, `Skipped` - instead of `IsFaithful`. "Clean" is derived from an empty claim list rather than stored, so the two cannot contradict each other. The disabled toggle now reports `Skipped` instead of claiming the output is faithful.
- **The model's answer is its own type.** `FaithfulnessVerdict` is the schema the model fills; `FaithfulnessReport` is what the pipeline acts on. That split is what lets the report express a state no model can report about itself, and it keeps the schema the model sees unchanged.
- **A verdict of unfaithful with no claims listed is also `NotEvaluated`.** It says something is wrong without saying what. Treating it as a clean check would hide the same failure a second way.
- **The run summary counts unreadable checks apart** from runs that genuinely found nothing, because both are an empty flag list and only a counter can tell them apart.

### Deliberately not in this PR

The run still exits 0. Whether an unverified check should fail a run belongs with the other exit-code findings from the v0.1.0 review - exit 0 when every audience fails, and `changelog.json` written from an empty result - which want deciding together rather than one case at a time.

changes.title: fix: leave breaking-change claims to the thorough check
changes.description:
## What does this PR do?

Removes the breaking-change claim check from `RuleBasedFaithfulnessChecker`. Breaking-change claims are now left to the thorough check.

The checker matched `\bbreaking\b` case-insensitively across the whole output and, when no fact was marked breaking, recorded *"The output claims a breaking change, but the facts mark none."* In the v0.1.0 dogfooding run it fired on all three audiences, every time on prose that legitimately described the breaking-change prominence setting or the check itself. The word appearing is not a claim being made.

## Why?

Same phrase-versus-assertion mistake #70 fixed in `ConventionalCommitCategorizer`, but the fix there does not transfer:

| | #70 | here |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Input | pull request body | LLM prose |
| Marker | Conventional Commits footer, defined form | none |
| Mention vs. declaration | syntactically decidable | a judgement |

Narrowing the footer regex made it *exact*, so precision and recall both improved. There is no equivalent move here: any narrowing just trades false positives for false negatives along a fuzzy boundary.

Anchoring to something the renderer emits was the option the issue favoured, but the renderer emits no structure of its own - `ReleaseRenderer` delegates to the generator, and `ChangelogFormatter` only normalizes bullets and blank lines. The only marker we control is the `(breaking)` string in the grounded facts, which the model is free not to carry over. That check would almost never fire, which is the same outcome as dropping it, with leftover code.

What is left in the layer asks one decidable question: is this token in the fact base or not. That is what makes it deterministic and free. The breaking check asked whether a sentence asserts something - interpretation wearing a regex. `ThoroughFaithfulnessChecker` already covers this: its prompt flags meaning-level distortions where the wording overstates what happened, and it already receives the `(breaking)` marker on the facts that carry it.

The trade is honest: with `faithfulness.thorough` off there is now no breaking-change check at all. That is acceptable because a flag that fired on every mention carried no signal - it cost reviewer attention and taught them to skip flags of that shape, including real ones.

Closes #71

changes.title: fix: two release blockers found by dogfooding v0.1.0
changes.description:
Found by running `chartula preview --tag v0.1.0` against this repository. Neither bug is reachable from the existing tests: the first needs a live API call, the second needs real pull request bodies.

## Truncation (`ChatModel`)

Calls went out without `ChatOptions`, so `MaxOutputTokens` was never set. The provider requires `max_tokens` and substitutes its own default of 1024 when absent. All three audience texts were cut off mid-word — the run metrics showed `3 calls, 3,072 out`, exactly 3 × 1024.

It failed silently. The run reported success, and the thorough check spent 56,712 tokens flagging the severed sentence as an unsupported claim — a real bug symptom read as a hallucination.

The ceiling is now always sent, configurable via `llm.maxOutputTokens`, defaulting to 16000.

## False breaking changes (`ConventionalCommitCategorizer`)

`MentionsBreakingChange` searched the whole body for `BREAKING CHANGE` as a case-insensitive substring, so prose *discussing* breaking changes *declared* one. Six of the thirty-three changes in v0.1.0 were mislabelled; none were breaking. #65 described a setting called breaking-change prominence and was marked breaking for saying so — the feature that renders breaking changes prominently became one.

Now matches the Conventional Commits footer: uppercase, start of line, colon-terminated.

## Verification

Both fixes confirmed against a real run, not just tests:

| | Before | After |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Rephrasing output | 3,072 tokens (3 × 1024) | 11,271 tokens |
| Text endings | mid-word | complete sentences |
| Breaking changes reported | 6 | 0 |
| Thorough check claims | 1 (the truncation artifact) | 0 |

265 tests pass, 9 new. The categorizer regression test uses the sentence from #65 verbatim as a fixture.

## Known, not fixed here

`RuleBasedFaithfulnessChecker` matches `\bbreaking\b` across the whole output and flags a breaking-change claim whenever the word appears — the same phrase-versus-assertion mistake, now visible because no fact is breaking anymore. The flags are advisory and do not fail a run, and separating a claim from prose that uses the word needs more than a regex. Filed separately rather than rushed in.

Phase 1 is complete, but the docs still described a project that was being planned.

- **CONTRIBUTING asked for "the .NET SDK"** - an older one cannot build `net10.0` - and documented four commit scopes (`collect`, `curate`, `render`, `check`) that were never used once, while the sixteen actually in use went unmentioned.

## What changed

**Long-celled tables became prose.** Two columns of paragraph text collapse on a phone, which is where a README often gets read. `Why Chartula`, `Core ideas` and `Roadmap` are now prose and headings. The tables that remain (env vars, doc index) hold short facts and survive a narrow column.

**Added [`docs/architecture.md`](docs/architecture.md).** The layering and the reasoning behind the dependency choices lived only in the code and in review comments, so nothing stopped a contributor from reaching for LibGit2Sharp or Octokit and quietly costing the native-AOT goal. It states the inward-pointing rule, why facts are established before an LLM sees them, and where each concern lives.

**Everything else now points somewhere**: a documentation index in the README, architecture and fixtures linked from CONTRIBUTING.

## Verification

- All 24 relative links in `README.md`, `CONTRIBUTING.md` and `docs/*.md` resolve to existing files.
- Both SVGs are valid XML with no external references and no `<script>`; rendered to PNG and checked against a dark and a light background.
- Uncommented every section of `chartula.example.yaml` into a real `chartula.yaml` and ran the CLI against it: all eight sections bind, no configuration error.

changes.title: feat: report what a run does and what it costs
changes.description:
Makes the tool measurable, so the defaults can be decided by data instead of guesswork.

Every `preview` and `generate` run now ends with:

```text
Run metrics
  Rule-based check: 3 runs, 1 with findings, 1 claim, no tokens
  Thorough check:   3 runs, 2 with findings, 2 claims, 6,230 in / 130 out
    caught 1 claim the rule-based check missed, for 6,360 tokens in 3 calls
  Rephrasing:       3 calls, 5,437 in / 859 out
  Total:            12,656 tokens
```

## Does the thorough check earn its cost?

The indented line is the point of the whole summary. It pairs the claims **only** the thorough check caught with the tokens it spent catching them. Claims both checks find are excluded, because on those the thorough check adds nothing over the free one. Read across a few real releases, that line answers the question directly: consistently zero claims caught means the tokens buy nothing.

## What changed

- `Chartula.Core/Observability/`: `IRunMetrics` with the `RunMetrics` sink, `NullRunMetrics`, `RunReport` and `RunReportFormatter`.
- `ChatModel` reports token usage, because it is the only place that sees it. Usage is attributed per `LlmOperation`, so the check's cost is readable on its own; a provider that reports no usage still has its call counted.
- `ReleasePipeline` records both checks' findings in one call, because it is the only place that can compare them, and returns the report on `ReleaseOutcome`.
- Measurement is a side channel: the sink is optional everywhere, and a run without one produces byte-identical output.
- `docs/run-metrics.md` explains how to read the summary and make the keep-or-drop call.

## Verification

- `dotnet build Chartula.slnx -c Debug`: 0 warnings, 0 errors.
- `dotnet test Chartula.slnx`: 215 passing (Core 177, Infrastructure 26, Cli 12), 21 of them new, covering check-fire counts, per-operation token usage, thorough-only attribution, snapshot isolation, and concurrent recording.
- CLI end-to-end: the real DI graph resolves the sink into both optional constructors, and the rendered summary was reviewed against the real formatter output.

## What

Gives the CLI a real command surface and ties the whole pipeline together.

- **`Chartula.Cli`**: `chartula preview` / `chartula generate`, each taking `--tag` and `--repo <owner/name>`; a usage screen; clear errors for unknown commands / missing options; a readable per-audience summary. Pipeline errors are caught and reported, not crashed.

changes.title: feat(output): write CHANGELOG.md, prepend and preserve history

## What

Writes each release as a new section at the top of `CHANGELOG.md`, preserving history and never overwriting it.

- **`Chartula.Cli`**: registers the writer alongside the JSON writer.

## Idempotency detail

Re-running a release replaces its section **in place** (keeping its position), so re-running an older release after a newer one doesn't move it above the newer one. Running the same release twice yields a byte-identical file.

changes.title: feat(faithfulness): rule-based check that catches obvious hallucinations

changes.title: feat(rendering): render technical, customer, and PM from one fact base

changes.title: feat(facts): transform curated changes into the release fact base

  - `LinkedIssues` are parsed from GitHub closing keywords (`closes/fixes/resolves #n`) in the title and body.

changes.title: feat(curation): degrade gracefully when clean PRs are missing
changes.description:
Closes #5

## What

Makes the pipeline still produce something useful when PR discipline is imperfect.

- **`Chartula.Core`**: `IReleaseChangeResolver` + `ReleaseChangeResolver` turn a `CommitRange` and the merged `PullRequestInfo` list into `ReleaseChange` values (title, description, number, url, labels, `ChangeSource`, commit sha). Pure domain logic, no I/O.
- **`Chartula.Cli`**: registers the resolver (dependency-free singleton).

## Behaviour

- Merged PRs present -> one change per PR (`Source = PullRequest`).
- No PRs at all -> one change per commit, using the commit subject (`Source = Commit`).
- Blank/uninformative PR title (e.g. `WIP`, `update`, `Merge ...`) -> falls back to the PR body's first informative line, then to a generic `PR #n`.
- Empty release -> empty set, never an exception.

The uninformative-title heuristic is a small starter set; it becomes configurable with the config work (#25).

## Acceptance criteria

- [x] With no associated PRs, the tool falls back to commit data.
- [x] With empty/uninformative PR titles, it uses the best available source.
- [x] The tool never hard-fails solely because PR discipline is imperfect.
- [x] Tests: cover each fallback path (no PRs, empty/uninformative titles) and confirm no hard failure.

changes.title: feat(pull-requests): fetch merged PRs for a release from the GitHub API
changes.description:
Closes #4

## What

Summarizes changes per merged PR instead of per raw commit.

- **`Chartula.Core`**: the `IReleasePullRequestReader` port plus `PullRequestInfo` (number, title, description, labels, url) and `RepositoryCoordinates`. Pure domain.
- **`Chartula.Infrastructure`**: `GitHubPullRequestReader` - for the commits in a `CommitRange`, queries GitHub's "pull requests associated with a commit" endpoint, keeps merged PRs only, de-duplicates by number. DTOs parsed via a source-generated `System.Text.Json` context.
- **`Chartula.Cli`**: composition root configures the `HttpClient` (base URL, GitHub headers, bearer token by env-var name) and registers the reader.

## Decisions

- **Raw `HttpClient` + `System.Text.Json` source-gen over Octokit** - dependency-light and native-AOT friendly (#39), consistent with the git-CLI choice in #3. The stub `HttpMessageHandler` makes it fully mockable without network.
- Token read by env-var name (`GITHUB_TOKEN`), optional (public repos work unauthenticated, subject to rate limits).

changes.description:
Closes #3

## What

Finds exactly the commits belonging to a release.

- **`Chartula.Core`**: the `IReleaseCommitReader` port plus `CommitInfo` and `CommitRange` (with `IsFirstRelease`). Pure domain, no I/O.
- **`Chartula.Infrastructure`** (new layer): `GitCliCommitReader` shells out to `git` - the range since the previous tag (`<prev>..<tag>`), or all history up to the tag when there is no previous tag (first release). Clear errors for unknown/blank tags.
- **`Chartula.Cli`**: composition root registers the git reader; the pipeline depends only on the port.

## Decisions

- **git CLI over LibGit2Sharp**: avoids native deps that would fight the planned native-AOT binaries (#39). `git` is present in any repo Chartula runs on.
- **New `Chartula.Infrastructure` layer** for concrete I/O adapters, keeping `Core` pure domain and `Cli` a thin composition root. Future home for the GitHub API (#4), file writers (#12/#20/#21), and webhooks (#28).

## Acceptance criteria

- [x] Given a tag, the commit range since the previous tag is determined.
- [x] Works when there is no previous tag (first release -> all history).
- [x] The commit set is available as input to the next stage (`CommitRange.Commits`, resolvable via `IReleaseCommitReader`).
- [x] Tests: cover the commit-range calculation, including the first-release case with no previous tag.

## Verification

Tests run the real `git` CLI against throwaway repositories (deterministic, offline): between-tags range, first-release fallback, sha/subject mapping, unknown-tag and blank-tag errors. Build 0 warnings / 0 errors; all tests green (Core 5, Infrastructure 6).

changes.title: feat(llm): abstract the LLM provider behind IChangelogModel
changes.description:
Closes #2

## What

Adds the provider-agnostic LLM seam the pipeline builds on.

- **`Chartula.Core`** (new): the domain-focused seam.
  - `IChangelogModel` - the interface the pipeline depends on (`RephraseAsync`, `CheckFaithfulnessAsync`).
  - `ChatModel` - the single implementation, backed by a provider-agnostic `Microsoft.Extensions.AI.IChatClient`.
  - Domain types: `Audience`, `GroundedFacts`, `RephraseRequest`, `FaithfulnessRequest`, `FaithfulnessReport`.
- **`Chartula.Cli`**: composition root wiring Anthropic as the first provider (`AsIChatClient`), model + provider selectable via config, API key read by env-var name. This is the only provider-specific code.
- **`Chartula.Core.Tests`** (new): 5 tests exercising the seam with a stub `IChatClient` - no live provider call.

## Acceptance criteria

- [x] An interface defines the LLM operations the pipeline needs.
- [x] At least one concrete provider implements it.
- [x] The rest of the code depends only on the interface.
- [x] API keys are read from environment/config, never hardcoded.
- [x] Tests: the seam is exercised with a stub IChatClient (no live provider call), asserting the pipeline uses only the interface.

## Notes

- Architecture chosen after discussion: hybrid (domain interface over agnostic `IChatClient`). Swapping providers is a composition-root change only.
- `GroundedFacts` and the `ChatModel` prompts are intentionally minimal placeholders; the fact base and prompt design are their own issues.

Build: 0 warnings / 0 errors. `dotnet test`: 5/5 green.

### What's New

- **Format rules in the prompt:** The customer prompt now includes four rules that govern the structure of changelog entries, ensuring consistency in the order of sections and the inclusion of required fields. This change was implemented to address formatting issues in the output and is tested using automated checks. Breaking changes are prioritized at the top, and migration links are correctly placed in the last group, aligning with the established format rules.
- **GitHub token warning:** A new CLI warning is displayed at startup when no GitHub token is found, informing users that the run will continue unauthenticated. This warning includes details about the GitHub rate limit and how setting a token increases the limit. Users are now directed to the correct method for setting the token using an environment variable.
- **Customer rendering as a page:** The customer rendering is now generated as a standalone page, `release-<tag>.md`, containing YAML front matter with metadata such as title, description, and date. This output is written locally and can be published separately, offering users a structured and customizable format for their changelogs.
- **Generate without publishing:** A new command-line option `--no-publish` is introduced, allowing users to generate `changelog.json` and `CHANGELOG.md` files without publishing the release notes. This option ensures that release notes are not inadvertently created for a tag that does not yet exist.
- **OpenAI-compatible provider:** A new provider option, `openai-compatible`, allows users to configure an endpoint that supports the OpenAI chat-completions protocol. This includes hosted endpoints and local servers, with flexibility to specify a custom base URL for the API. Users are now prompted to configure both the model and base URL when using this provider.
- **Thinking configuration:** A new configuration option `llm.thinking` allows users to specify whether the model should engage in thinking, remain disabled, or use an adaptive strategy. This setting impacts token consumption and cost, influencing the thoroughness of the analysis performed by the model.
- **Run metrics summary:** A new metric summary is added at the end of `preview` and `generate` runs, detailing the number of tokens used in different phases of processing such as rule-based checks, thorough checks, and rephrasing. This helps users understand the cost and efficiency of their runs.
- **Category configuration:** A new configuration section in `chartula.yaml` enables users to define custom categories, their order, and display names. This includes controlling whether breaking changes are highlighted, providing greater flexibility in how changelogs are structured and presented.
- **Configuration from YAML:** The tool now reads configuration from a `chartula.yaml` file, defaulting to sensible behaviors when no configuration is provided. An example file is included to guide users in customizing the behavior of the tool according to their needs.
- **Preview and generate commands:** The CLI now supports `preview` and `generate` commands that tie into the entire pipeline, allowing users to simulate or write output without publishing. These commands ensure consistent behavior across development and deployment workflows.
- **Write to GitHub release notes:** Generated text is now written directly to the GitHub release notes, updating existing releases instead of creating new ones. This ensures that release notes are kept accurate and up-to-date without duplication.
- **Prepend to CHANGELOG.md:** The `CHANGELOG.md` file is now updated by prepending new sections at the top, preserving the historical entries. This prevents overwriting previous data and ensures a clear and continuous changelog.
- **Review mode for flagged passages:** A review mode is added that allows users to review flagged sections in the generated texts before they are finalized. This provides an opportunity for human verification or correction of any content before publication.
- **Thorough faithfulness check:** A new configuration option `faithfulness.thorough` enables or disables a more detailed check for semantic accuracy in the generated text, ensuring that unsupported claims are identified and corrected.
- **Rule-based hallucination check:** A rule-based check is introduced that automatically flags obvious hallucinations such as unsupported numbers, quoted names, or breaking-change claims that are not present in the fact base. This check is always on and does not require any LLM calls.
- **Multi-audience rendering:** The tool now renders technical, customer, and product-manager versions of the release from the same fact base, ensuring consistency across all audiences and eliminating contradictions in the output.
- **Prompt rephrasing rules:** The prompting architecture is restructured to ensure that the LLM strictly rephrases information without introducing new facts. The prompt now instructs the model to use only the provided information, focusing on rephrasing and avoiding any guesswork.
- **Provider-agnostic generation:** Generation through the LLM now works via the provider interface, ensuring compatibility across different providers without requiring direct provider-specific code. This allows for flexible switching between different LLMs while keeping the implementation provider-agnostic.
- **Fact base depth configuration:** The depth of information included in the fact base is now configurable, allowing users to choose between title-only, title and description, or title, description, and linked issues. This customization helps tailor the fact base to the project's documentation style.
- **Fact base from curated changes:** A fact base is assembled from curated changes, capturing essential details such as title, category, linked issues, and user visibility. This fact base serves as the structured data upon which all subsequent processing and rendering are based.
- **Fact base data model:** A structured data model is defined for each change, encapsulating information like title, number, link, category, and linked issues. This model ensures that all relevant details are captured deterministically without relying on the LLM for any information.
- **Filtering internal changes:** Internal and chore changes are excluded by default from the changelog, enhancing its relevance to users by excluding non-user-visible changes. This behavior can be overridden by configuration to include such changes if needed.
- **Label-based curation:** Curation is now guided by label rules from the configuration file, enabling users to filter changes based on GitHub labels, assign categories, or include only labeled changes. This provides a way to influence the curation process without modifying code.
- **Deterministic categorization:** Changes are categorized deterministically based on Conventional Commit prefixes, ensuring consistent classification without involving the LLM. This prevents the model from introducing incorrect or guessed categories.
- **Graceful fallback for missing PRs:** The tool gracefully degrades when clean PRs are missing, using commit data as fallback instead of failing entirely. This ensures that the changelog is produced even in the absence of fully formed PRs.
- **Use merged PRs for changes:** Merged PRs are now used to summarize changes instead of raw commits, providing better context for each change. This is achieved by querying the GitHub API for the PRs associated with a commit range, extracting relevant information efficiently.
- **Commit range from Git:** The commit range for a release is determined by reading from the Git CLI, ensuring accurate tracking of commits from the previous release to the current one. This provides a clear and reliable method for capturing the relevant commits for each release.
- **Provider abstraction:** The LLM provider is abstracted behind an interface, allowing for swapping between different providers without affecting the rest of the tool. This abstraction ensures that the tool remains flexible and can work with various LLMs while maintaining a consistent API.

### Bug Fixes

- **Preserve body when no description:** A bug fix ensures that when no description is present, the text is not incorrectly lifted out of the body, preserving the integrity of the generated content. This fix prevents the rendering from being lost when the description is the only text present.
- **Outcome slot requirement:** The prompt now requires the outcome slot in every entry, ensuring that users can always rely on a clear statement of what they can now expect. This change enforces the structural integrity of each changelog entry, preventing incomplete or ambiguous statements.
- **Customer entry structure:** Customer audience entries are now required to follow a specific structural format, including the mandatory inclusion of four parts in each entry. This ensures consistency in how changes are described and communicated to the end users.
- **Distinguish unreadable checks:** Unreadable thorough checks are now clearly distinguished from clean checks in the run metrics, helping users identify when the system failed to interpret the model's response. This distinction improves the clarity of the run output and avoids misleading reports of no findings.
- **Breaking-change check focus:** Breaking-change claims are now left exclusively to the thorough check, avoiding false positives in the rule-based check. This adjustment ensures that only meaningful breaking changes are flagged, improving the accuracy of the system's responses.
- **Distinguish LLM calls:** A distinction is now made between unreported LLM calls and standard calls, making the run metrics more informative. This allows for better tracking and analysis of the model's behavior and output.
- **Fix truncation and breaking change issues:** Two issues were identified and fixed by running the tool against the v0.1.0 release of the repository. These included a truncation problem due to missing token limits and incorrect identification of breaking changes in certain pull request descriptions.
